newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Tristao ups 97/98 coffee estimate 8.94 pct.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Tristao ups 97/98 coffee estimate 8.94 pct.

text.p: Brazilian trade house Tristao has increased its estimate for Brazil's 1997/98 coffee crop to 25.6 million 60-kg bags, up 8.94 percent from an April forecast of 23.5 million bags.

The latest figure compares with an unchanged estimate of 27.5 million bags in 1996/97 and follows a field trip throughout various coffee regions in the country during the initial period of the present harvest.
Of the new total, arabica coffee is expected to account for 20.75 million bags, against 18.55 million bags in April.
Robusta production has actually been revised downwards slightly in the latest estimate to 4.85 million bags from 4.95 million bags previously.
The biggest increase by state is in Minas Gerais, now expected to produce 12.3 million bags, up from an April forecast of 10.6 million bags.
Sao Paulo output is also now seen higher at 3.5 million bags compared with 3.2 million bags in April.
The overall increase is due to a number of factors including favorable climatic conditions for the final maturation of the cherries, even though the recent rainfall has affected quality.
There has also been careful treatment and adequate investments during the harvest, the company said in a report.

Yields are now expected to be higher than initially anticipated in that a lower volume of cherries will be needed to obtain one bag of green coffee. This is especially true in Minas Gerais, Sao Paulo and Parana.
The quality is at this moment the most important factor to be considered and according to Tristao's surveys, this crop will have a high percentage of large arabica and conillon beans.

However the large amount of rain in certain regions during June, especially in south Minas Gerais and Parana, will generate a considerable amount of rain-damaged coffees, causing therefore a drop in type standard and cup of this crop.
During June, some 96 millimeters of rain fell in south Minas Gerais and 430 millimeters in Parana, Tristao said.
This compares with 30 millimeters and 13.5 millimeters for each region respectively in the same month in 1996 and nine millimeters and 67 millimeters in 1995.
As for conillons, there has been a substantial increase in bean damage caused by broca, mainly in Espirito Santo, causing a drop in yield, Tristao said.
A breakdown by state follows. All figures are in '000 bags.
